How to account for clustering and nesting in biological data analyses

Erik Parker, Lijiang Guo, Beate Henschel, Xiwei Chen, Lilian Golzarri Arroyo and Stephanie Dickinson for the Biostatistics Consulting Center (BCC)

18 May 2026

Introduction

In aging research, preclinical studies often rely on animal models to evaluate the effects of interventions on lifespan and healthspan. A persistent methodological challenge in these studies is the failure to account for clustering and nesting effects inherent in experimental designs. Clustering arises when observations within a group or shared environment, such as animals housed in the same cage, may exhibit correlated outcomes. Nesting refers to a hierarchical data structure where clusters (e.g. cages) are nested within treatment, resulting from a cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT).

  • Clustering arises when observations within a group or shared environment, such as animals housed in the same cage, students in the same school, or repeated measures taken on the same subject. The clusters are often known as levels of a factor (e.g. cage id’s of the factor cage, school id’s of the factor school, or subject id’s of the factor subject). When a group of observations belong to the same level of a factor, the level would induce correlations among those observation.
  • Nesting refers to a hierarchical data structure where clusters (e.g. cages) are nested within treatment. In this case, a factor’s levels cluster under another factor’s levels. For example, for cages housing animals, each cage belongs to one treatment level. Because cages are now partitioned by treatment, a group of cages would belong to the same level of treatment, which would induce a correlation structure among those cages.


Figure 1: Possible designs for registry randomised controlled trials. ICU, intensive care unit; RCT, randomised controlled trial.
(image source: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/13/3/e068057)


When clustering in the data is ignored in analysis, standard errors of estimates may be artificially reduced, such that there is an increased risk of Type I errors (1–6). Similarly, false positives (Type I error) can result from using degrees of freedom at the level of the individual animal rather than the number of cages in the context of nesting from a cRCT (9). Despite decades of methodological guidance (7,10), clustering and nesting effects are still frequently overlooked in preclinical studies, including those in aging research, and more must be done to account for these effects to achieve valid statistical inference (11).

Fortunately, statistical methods such as linear mixed models, generalized estimating equations, and Cox frailty models provide researchers with robust tools to account for clustering and nesting effects using widely available software packages such as R and SAS (8,12,13). These methods extend standard approaches by modeling dependencies within clusters, ensuring that statistical conclusions accurately reflect the true structure of the data. However, as in other fields, we observe that researchers in the aging field often fail to account for clustering and nesting, underscoring the need for greater statistical rigor.

This tutorial, and our associated paper (14,15), illustrate methods that can be used to account for clustering and nesting using recent data from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP), a multi-site initiative investigating the effects of various compounds on lifespan in genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 mice, as a case study (16).

Below we demonstrate how both R and SAS can be used to extend classical statistical methods to account for clustering and nesting effects. All examples include relevant code, commented to explain what is being done and why. All code chunks are hidden by default, but can be shown by clicking the “Show” button above the table results.

To download the data to run this tutorial, see our OSF site at https://osf.io/rgm2s/overview. Also, see the github repository for this page at https://github.com/BCC-iu/Clustering-and-nesting-tutorial.

Case Study using ITP Survival Data

The 2019 ITP data used in this analysis was generated from an experiment testing the effects of multiple compounds on lifespan in UM-HET3 mice housed at three test sites: University of Michigan(UM), University of Texas (UT), and the Jackson Laboratory (TJL) (16). Briefly, mice were weaned at 42 days of age and assigned to a cage, after which cages were then randomized using a block design. All cage hold 3-4 mice with the exception of 2 cages which hold 2 mice. All mice within the same cage were given the same treatment (as it was included in their food), and randomization was done separately for male and female animals at each test site. There were 777 total cages spread across the three test sites. The treatments used in this study (in addition to the control group) were Astaxanthin (Asta), Meclizine (Mec), Dimethyl fumarate (DMF), Mycophenolic acid (MPA), 4-Phenylbutyrate (PBA), and SG1002 – a hydrogen sulfide donor. Below we show the number of mice and cages in each site and each treatment. Full information on the mice rearing methods can be found in (16).

First we will load in and clean the data, first in R:

knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

library(tidyverse) # for manipulating data
library(kableExtra) # for making general tables
library(gtsummary) # for making model tables
library(table1)
library(lmerTest) # for fitting linear mixed models
library(readxl) # for loading in excel files
library(performance) # for calculating ICC values
library(survival) # for survival analyses
library(survminer) # for KM plots
library(broom) # for tidying model fit statistics
library(broom.mixed) # for tidying linear mixed model stats
library(coxme) # fit cox model with nested random effects
#devtools::install_github('junkka/ehahelper') # to extract model information from coxme model
library(ehahelper) # to extract model information from coxme model
library(emmeans) # for getting estimated marginal means
library(patchwork) # package for putting plots together
library(SASmarkdown) # for running SAS code in chunks

# set up the options so that knit knows where the SAS executable is
saspath <- "C:/Program Files/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/sas.exe"


ITP.data <- read_xlsx("../Data/C2019 raw with cage numbers 2023-07-24.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(Site = factor(Site),
         Cage = factor(Cage),
         Sex = factor(Sex),
         Rx = factor(Rx, 
                     levels = c("Cont_19",
                                "Asta",
                                "DMF_16",
                                "DMF_early",
                                "MEC",
                                "MPA",
                                "PBA",
                                "SG1002_2"))) %>%
  unite(col = "Cage_site", c("Cage", "Site"), remove = FALSE)
# read in the data and set factor variables
# as of 2023-09-22 I'm adding a new variable, Cage_site, which is a combination of cage and site. Doing this because Rich Miller emailed that cages are repeated across different sites.
# also I am now reordering the drug variable now that we have more information about what the different drugs are. Control is Cont_19 and is now the reference level.

ITP.data.long <- ITP.data %>%
    group_by(UMN) %>% # group by animal
    complete(Age = seq(1, max(Age))) %>% # add in rows for all days alive for each animal
    fill(Cage_site, Rx, Sex, Dead, .direction = "updown") %>% # fill in the covariate info
    select(UMN, Age, Cage_site, Sex, Rx, Dead) %>% # select just the few variables I want
  ungroup() %>% # remove ID grouping
  group_by(Cage_site, Age) %>% # group by age and cage, will let us calculate the number of animals alive at each day, per cage
  mutate(num_cagemates_alive = length(unique(UMN)) - 1,
         num_cagemates_alive = factor(num_cagemates_alive,
                                      levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3"))) %>% # add a new variable for number of cagemates alive at each day, changes over time as animals die
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(UMN) %>% # group by animal again
  mutate(mort = ifelse(Age == max(Age) & Dead == 1, 1, 0)) # make a new variable "mort" which is 1 if a mouse dies on a given day and 0 otherwise. This will be the outcome for the time varying models
# make a "long" form of the data that has one row for each day alive for each mouse. This will be used in plotting and for models


ITP.data.cox <- ITP.data.long %>% # take the long data
  group_by(UMN) %>%
    mutate(stop = max(Age)) %>% # new variable that Surv() function looks for, "stop" which specifies the last age recorded for each animal
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(UMN, num_cagemates_alive) %>% # group by subject and the number of cagemates alive
  slice_head() %>% # take one row per animal, per number of cagemates alive. This will slice the data at the timepoint/age when the number of cagemates alive changes.
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(start = 0) %>% # add a new variable "start" for each animal which specifies that each animal started at age/time 0.
  arrange(UMN, Age) %>% # arrange the data so age is ascending within animal
  group_by(UMN) %>% # group by animal
  mutate(tstart = ifelse(Age == 1, Age - 1, Age), # interval start time either 0 (Age - 1) if it's the first interval, or the time of the interval start
         tstop = lead(Age), # interval stop time is the NEXT row's time.
         tstop = ifelse(is.na(tstop), stop, tstop), # make new variables that Surv() looks for. These are the start and stop time for each interval, with the intervals defined by if the number of cagemates alive changes
         mort = ifelse(tstop == stop & Dead == 1, 1, 0)) %>% # update the "mort", endpoint variable to be 1 if the animal died at the end of the given interval. 0 if they didn't
  filter(!c(tstart == tstop & mort == 1)) # remove rows created in error where the start and stop time of the interval were the same days, and the animal was already recorded as dead.
# make the time varying cox model dataset

ITP.data.lmm <- ITP.data.cox %>%
  group_by(UMN) %>%
  mutate(Age.at.change = ifelse(mort == 1, tstop, lead(Age))) %>%
  filter(Dead == 1)
# make a different dataset specific to the time varying covariate cox model with time varying covariates, this one will use Age.at.change as the outcome where that age can either be the time of death, or the time at which the number of cagemates changes.

Then in SAS:


%let filepath=C:\ITP cages\Data;

data _null_;

   today = put(date(), YYMMDDD10.);*this returns the date in the format 2022-09-08;

   call symput('today',today);

run;*use in code as &today.;

%put &today.;

/*************************************************** Read in Dataset ***************************************************/

PROC IMPORT OUT= WORK.ITP_data

           DATAFILE= "&filepath.\C2019 raw with cage numbers 2023-07-24.xlsx"

            DBMS=EXCEL REPLACE;

    RANGE="UM C2019 LT 10-12-22$";

     GETNAMES=YES;

     MIXED=NO;

     SCANTEXT=YES;

     USEDATE=YES;

     SCANTIME=YES;

RUN;

/* make a new Cage_site variable for clustering, and then filter the data to include just the non-censored animals, like the paper did */

data WORK.ITP_data;

    set WORK.ITP_data;

    Cage_site = Cage || Site;

   drop F11 F12 F13 F14 F15 F16 F17 F18 F19 F20 F21 F22 F23 F24 F25 F26 F27 F28 F29 F30 F31 F32 F33 F34 ;

run;

data WORK.ITP_filtered_data;

   set WORK.ITP_data;

   IF Dead = 1 THEN OUTPUT;

run;

Now we can look at some descriptive tables of the sample, using R code:

my.render.cat <- function(x) {
    c("", sapply(stats.default(x), function(y) with(y,
        sprintf("%d", FREQ))))
}
label(ITP.data$Rx) <- "Treatment"

cell_mice <- as.data.frame(table1(~Rx|Site, data=ITP.data, render.categorical=my.render.cat, overall = F) )
cell_cage <- as.data.frame(table1(~Rx|Site, data=ITP.data |> group_by(Cage_site) |> filter(row_number()==1) |> ungroup(), render.categorical=my.render.cat, overall = F)) 
cell_mice_cage <- as.data.frame(mapply(function(x, y) paste0(x, " (", y, ")"), cell_mice, cell_cage)) |>
  filter(!row_number()%in%c(1,2)) 
cell_mice_cage[,1] <- cell_mice[3:10,1] 
cell_mice_cage |>
  kable(caption="<center>Number of Animals (Cages) in each Treatment x Site</center>", align="c") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = T)

Descriptive Statistics

As a first starting point when working with data, we generally want to look at some basic descriptive statistics. We have descriptive statistics for survival time by treatment, sex, and site - along with exploratory plots of survival time by treatment.

Descriptive statistics of survival time

Three tables of mean, median, IQR, max, and min of survival time by Rx, site, and sex combinations.

# below to make tables for descriptive data

ITP.data %>% # take the dataset
    select(Rx, Sex, Age) %>% # select just the treatment, sex and age variables
    tbl_strata( # make a stratified table
        strata = Sex, # that is stratified by sex
        ~.x %>%
            tbl_summary( # within each sex strata, make a summary table
                by = Rx, # that is further stratified by treatment
                statistic = list(Age ~ "{mean};  {median};  ({p25}, {p75});  ({min}, {max})") # report this list of statistics 
            ),
        modify_header(all_stat_cols() ~ "**{level}**"), # label each table strata with the level of the "by =" variable level
        .header = "**{strata}**, N = {n}" # then label the top level strata by the "strata =" variable level
    )

Intra-Class Correlation

Because we are dealing with nested/clustered data, we are also presenting calculations of Intraclass correlation (ICC) values for both cage and site clusters. From these ICC values, we can see that if we only account for the similarity between sites, we are missing ~10% of the variation that can be explained just from the cages, or cages within sites. Because of this, we know that it is important to properly account for both cages and sites within our modeling framework.

ICC by cage and site 
ITP.data.dead <- ITP.data %>%
  filter(Dead == 1)

mod.cage <- lmer(Age ~ 1 + (1 | Cage_site), data = ITP.data.dead)
# fit a intercept only model on the outcome (Age at death) which includes a random intercept for cage.

ICC.cage <- performance::icc(mod.cage)
# return the ICC for cage, this gives the same value as manually doing Variance between / (Variance between + Variance within) like so:
# print(VarCorr(mod.site), comp = "Variance") to get the variances and 6816 / (6816 + 49176) to calculate it.


mod.site <- lmer(Age ~ 1 + (1 | Site), data = ITP.data.dead)
# fit a intercept only model on the outcome (Age at death) which includes a random intercept for site

ICC.site <- performance::icc(mod.site)
# return the ICC for site

mod.site.cage <- lmer(Age ~ 1 + (1 | Site / Cage_site), data = ITP.data.dead)
# fit a intercept only model on the outcome (Age at death) which includes a random intercept for site

ICC.site.cage <- performance::icc(mod.site.cage)
# return the ICC for site by cage clustering

# put it all together into a data frame
data.frame("Clustering variable" = c("Cage", "Site", "Site by cage"),
           "Average per cluster" = c(round(ITP.data.dead %>% group_by(Cage_site) %>% mutate(count = n()) %>% slice_head() %>% ungroup() %>% summarise("mean mice per Cage" = mean(count)) %>% as.numeric(), 2),
                                     round(ITP.data.dead %>% group_by(Site) %>% mutate(count = n()) %>% slice_head() %>% ungroup() %>% summarise("mean mice per Site" = mean(count)) %>% as.numeric(),2),
                                     round(ITP.data.dead %>% group_by(Site, Cage_site) %>% mutate(count = n()) %>% slice_head() %>% ungroup() %>% summarise("mean mice per Site per cage" = mean(count)) %>% as.numeric(),2)),
           ICC = c(round(ICC.cage$ICC_unadjusted, 3), 
                   round(ICC.site$ICC_unadjusted,3),
                   round(ICC.site.cage$ICC_unadjusted,3))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Clustering variable", "Average per cluster", "ICC"), 
        caption="<center>Overall ICC for all samples</center>", align="l") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = T)

        caption="<center>Overall ICC for females</center>", align="l") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = T)

Under the hood

These ICC values were calculated from a simple linear mixed model of form (Age ~ 1 + (1 | cluster)) where cluster was either site or cage. From there we used the formula \[\frac{ \text{Var}_{\text{within}} } { \text{Var}_{\text{between}} + \text{Var}_{\text{within}} }\] to obtain the ICC values listed below. This formula is the standard way to calculate intraclass correlation coefficients in mixed models and corresponds to ICC(1,1) given by Shrout & Fleiss (17) as \[\text{ICC} =\frac{ \sigma^2_{r} } { \sigma^2_{r} + \sigma^2_{v} }\] where \(\sigma^2_{r}\) is between cluster group variance and \(\sigma^2_{v}\) is within cluster group variance.


Back to top

Linear Mixed Models

We fit linear models as a baseline where the number of days alive was treated as a continuous outcome on only the non-censored animals. To assess the impact of cage clustering effects, we fit linear mixed models, with random intercepts for cage nested within treatment where the number of days alive was treated as a continuous outcome for all non-censored animals. Cage nested within treatment was included as a random intercept to capture the degree to which animals housed in the same cage might have survival times more similar to each other than to animals housed in some other cage, due to “random”, unmeasured factors that are not accounted for in the model. Denominator degrees of freedom were adjusted using the Kenward-Roger approximation to be at the level of the number of cages rather than individual animals. Statistical significance of the interaction term and main effects were assessed using type 3 sum of squares, and estimated marginal means were compared to assess significant differences in lifespan between each treatment group and the control group within each sex.

Below we have results from linear models which do not account for cage and site nesting and clustering effects, and linear mixed models which do account for these effects using the Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom approximation. These results are presented using both R and SAS code.

Fitted Models

Below we see results of R and SAS. For both the R and SAS code sections we first see the results for the linear models (not accounting for cage and site effects), and then for the linear mixed models which do properly account for cage and site.

R results

We use the lmer() function from the lmerTest package in R to fit the linear mixed model. The model lmer(Age ~ Rx * Sex + (1 | Cage_site : Rx) + (1 | Site) adjusts for the clustering effects of cage and the nesting effect of treatment and sites. Comparing the results from summary() in linear model and linear mixed models, the standard errors of the coefficients have increased when the clustering and nesting have been accounted and hence Type I error rate is reduced.

First we fit a linear model which does not adjust for the cage clusters, or the fact that treatment is nested within sites. Then, we look at the results of that model using the summary() command.

# fit linear model
lm.noclus <- lm(Age ~ Rx * Sex, data = ITP.data.no.cen)
summary(lm.noclus)

Then we fit the linear mixed model by loading the lmerTest package and using the lmer() function from said package. Here we are using lmerTest instead of the alternative, lmer package as it provides p-values by default in the summary() results table. As before, we are fitting the model and then examining the results.

library(lmerTest) # first load the lmerTest package for fitting the mixed models, using the lmer command
# fit the mixed model
lmm.cage <- lmer(Age ~ Rx * Sex + (1 | Cage_site : Rx) + (1 | Site), data = ITP.data.no.cen)
summary(lmm.cage)

SAS results

In SAS we use the PROC MIXED command to fit the linear and linear mixed models. When we fit the linear models the random statement is omitted, but is included when we fit the linear mixed model. Note that just like in the R code we are choosing to use the Kenward-Roger’s degrees of freedom approximation.

Note here that the default SAS output contains different pieces of information as compared to the default R output from the summary() command. Both have beta estimates, standard errors, and p-values for each term. But, the SAS output additionally also contains estimated degrees of freedom for each term in the fixed effect table, along with additional tables for the structure of the model - and the table of type 3 F-test results which we will focus on in the next section.


/* below to fit the standard linear model which is the equivalent of the R linear model fit before  */

PROC MIXED data = ITP_filtered_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site;

   model Age = Rx Sex Rx * Sex / solution ;

RUN;

/* below to fit the linear mixed model which is the equivalent of the R mixed model fit before, here also using Kenward-Roger DF approximation  */

PROC MIXED data = ITP_filtered_data covtest;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Site Cage_site;

   model Age = Rx Sex Rx * Sex / solution DDFM = KENWARDROGER;

   random intercept / subject=Cage_site(Rx) ;*type = un;

   random intercept / subject=Site ;*type = un;

RUN;

Type 3 F-tests

Below we see results of type 3 F-tests for R and SAS. Note how the p-values, F-values, and especially the denominator degrees of freedom differ between the models - which reflects the Kenward-Rogers DF adjustment such that they are roughly on the order of the number of cages.

R results

In the Type 3 Anova tables, the degrees of freedom using the Kenward-Roger method are smaller than before, and the p-values are bigger.

From these tables we see that the interactions between sex and treatment are never statistically significant (i.e., p < 0.05) - meaning that the treatments do not appear to differentially affect survival time in male and female animals. Put another way, the effect of treatment on lifespan does not depend on the sex of the animal.

However, we do see that in both the linear and linear mixed models that the main effects of treatment and sex are both statistically significant. This tells us that there is a significant impact of both treatment and sex on survival time, when averaged across the levels of the other variable. That is, we see that there is a significant difference in survival time between male and female animals (in both the linear: p < 0.001, and linear mixed: p < 0.001) models regardless of what treatment they receive. And we can say the same for treatment, where we see a significant difference in survival time based on treatment in both models (linear: p = 0.002, and linear mixed: p = 0.011) regardless of which sex the animal is.

# fit the type 3 sum of squares anova for the linear model
lm.anova <- car::Anova(lm.noclus, type = 3)
print(lm.anova)

SAS results

As noted in the R section above, the SAS code also shows non-significant interaction terms, significant main effects, and increased p-values when we fit the linear mixed vs. standard linear model.

Also note that the default way to show type 3 tests in SAS provides much more information than the R output above - but also note that the p-values are quite comparable to the R analysis.


/* below to fit the standard linear model which is the equivalent of the R linear model fit before  */

PROC MIXED data = ITP_filtered_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site;

   model Age = Rx Sex Rx * Sex / solution ;

RUN;

Under the hood

In Linear Mixed Models (LMM), the exact null distribution for the parameter estimates and hence test statistics are unknown. It is appropriate to use the Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT), but it has been found to produce anti-conservative p-values. Simulation based alternatives such as boot straping is computationally expensive. The lmertest::anova function provides F and t tests with approximated null distribution. Two common approximation methods are Satterthwaite’s method for denominator degrees of freedom and Kenward-Roger’s method for covariance matrix of the estimated fixed effects.

A LRT of LMM hypothesis is constructed as \(H_0: \theta_0 \in \Theta_0\) and \(H_1:\theta_1 \in \Theta_1\) where \(\Theta_0 \subset \Theta_1\): \[L = -2(\text{log-likelihood}(\Theta_0) - \text{log-likelihood}(\Theta_1)),\] where \(\Theta_0\) and \(\Theta_1\) are parameter spaces of null and alternative hypotheses respectively. This L statistic is compared to a \(\chi^2\) distribution of \(||\theta_1|| - ||\theta_0||\) degrees of freedom. In general this test is asymptotically correct, but frequently produce anti-conservative \(p\) values and inflated type 1 error rate.

In the F test of hypothesis \(H_0: L\beta = 0\) where \(L\) is a contrast matrix of \(\text{rank}(L) = q > 1\), the test statistic is defined as:

\[F = \frac{(L\hat\beta)^T(L\hat{C}L^T)^{-1}(L\hat\beta)}{q},\] where C is variance-covariance matrix of \(\beta\). A naive Wald F test would compare this F statistic to a F distribution with \(q\) and \(n-q\) degrees of freedom where \(q\) is the number of fixed effects being tested and \(n\) is the sample size. A t test of \(\beta_i = 0\) would follow as: \[t = \sqrt{F} = \frac{\hat{\beta_i}}{\sqrt{\hat{V}(\hat{\beta_i})}}.\] A naive t test would compare this t statistic to a t distribution with \(1, n-q\) degrees of freedom.

Even though the statistic is called F or t, in general it does not exactly follow an F or t distribution. Satterthwaite method uses a method of moment approach to estimate denominator degrees of freedom \(\nu\) such that \(F \sim F_{q,\nu}\).

In Kenward-Roger’s method the estimated variance-covariance matrix \(\hat{C}\) is adjusted in order to improve the small sample distributional properties of F and then the Satterthwaite’s method-of-moment of approximation is applied.

Additionally, for more details on the way in which these degrees of freedom methods are implemented in R specifically, see our other in-depth tutorial here: [link to Lijiang anova study tutorial]

Estimated Marginal Means

After looking for the presence of statistically significant overall effects (such as treatment or sex effects), it is often of interest to investigate pairwise relationships in the data.

Below we present linear mixed model-informed estimated marginal means and standard errors for each treatment group, separated by sex. That is, what does our linear mixed model estimate as the average survival time within each treatment group, for male animals specifically. Further, we also present p-values from pairwise comparisons of each treatment mean vs. the control - as a way of testing if any particular group shows significantly different longevity as compared to the control group.

As before, we present both R and SAS code below.

R results

Previously we saw that there was not a significant interaction term in either the linear or linear mixed models, but that we saw significant effects of both sex and treatment. To understand where those significant effects are coming from, we then want to look at specific estimates of survival time for our individual sex and treatment groups. Further, and as mentioned above, we also want to compare the estimates for each treatment within each sex to see if there are any pairwise differences.

In cases where we have set control and treatment groups it’s likely of most interest to see how each treatment compares to the control - so here we mostly want to focus on how much longer each treatment group survives on average as compared to the control, within each sex.

And from looking at the R results we see there are no significant pairwise differences in female animals, but that male animals given Asta or MEC survive significantly longer than the controls in the linear (p = 0.0001 and 0.0013), and linear mixed (p = 0.0003 and 0.0029) models. Note that as before with the type 3 F-test results, properly accounting for clustering/nesting effects using the mixed models and subsequently adjusting the degrees of freedom using the Kenward-Rogers method results in larger, more conservative, p-values.

# get the emmeans for the linear model
emm.noclus <- emmeans(lm.noclus, pairwise ~ Rx | Sex, adjust = "none")
print(emm.noclus)

SAS results

As above, we see that the default SAS output is more verbose, but that it generally matches the R results quite closely. Note though that outside of the purposes of this tutorial SAS does have the advantage of being able to include multiple arguments in a single PROC MIXED call, such that you would be able to display the model estimates, type 3 F-tests, estimated marginal means (lsmeans in SAS), and more by simply adding the necessary lines to your PROC MIXED call - while R’s object-oriented programming style is more modular and flexible and often requires the use of multiple packages and lines of code to reproduce SAS’ output.

Neither R nor SAS has a “better” approach for these kinds of analyses per-se, they just each prioritize different aspects of analysis. Flexibility, modularity, and “third-party” extensions (packages) for R, and “first-party” completeness for SAS.


/* below to fit the standard linear model which is the equivalent of the R linear model fit before  */

PROC MIXED data = ITP_filtered_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site;

   model Age = Rx Sex Rx * Sex / ;

   lsmeans Rx * Sex / diff cl;

RUN;

/* below to fit the linear mixed model which is the equivalent of the R mixed model fit before, here also using Kenward-Roger DF approximation  */

PROC MIXED data = ITP_filtered_data covtest;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Site Cage_site;

   model Age = Rx Sex Rx * Sex / DDFM = KENWARDROGER;

   random intercept / subject=Cage_site(Rx) ;*type = un;

   random intercept / subject=Site ;*type = un;

   lsmeans Rx * Sex / diff cl;

RUN;

Cox Models

Then, because survival data are a special class of time to event data in which subjects can either encounter or undergo the event of interest (death, in survival analyses) or not during the observation period, we wanted to use analysis methods specifically designed for these types of data. Here we are using Cox Proportional Hazards (PH) models for this purpose.

Cox PH models allow researchers to properly account for multiple complexities of time to event data, including the fact that these data are often not normally distributed, show non-constant risks of event occurrence over time, and can contain “censored” subjects for whom the event of interest was not observed during the study period. These models are very useful, but unfortunately do not allow for proper modeling of nested or clustered data. However, like before with linear models and mixed models - the Cox PH model can also be extended to handle clustered and nested data structures through the use of frailty terms.

The frailty model is an extension of the standard Cox PH model which incorporates random effects (the frailty terms), much like the linear mixed model, to account for dependence, correlations, or unobserved relationships within the data (18). These frailty models were fit using both gamma and Gaussian distributions for the random effect frailty terms of cage nested within treatment. The gamma and Gaussian distributions are both commonly used but have different mathematical characteristics and may perform better in certain scenarios (18). Because we did not have an a priori reason to believe one would perform better than the other, we used both distributions here and compared the results of the two. Degrees of freedom for the Cox frailty models are estimated following (19). Type 3 sums of squares were used to assess the significance of the interaction term and main effects, and estimated marginal means were calculated and compared to assess significant differences in death hazards between each treatment group and the control group within each sex.

Below we have both R and SAS output for these Cox PH and frailty models.

Note that the R output differs slightly from the SAS output for the Cox models. This is because the two R packages for frailty models (survival and coxme) have different issues that make it so we can’t exactly match SAS. Coxme can only fit gaussian distribution models, not gamma, and it treats the random effects differently than SAS does, so the type 3 tables give slightly different results. The survival package can fit gamma and gaussian frailty models, but the models don’t support the Car::Anova() function well, so we can’t get an accurate type 3 sum of squares F-test from them, and so can’t match that from SAS. Because it is better described and more flexible, the SAS output was used for the tables in our paper.

Back to top

Type 3 LR Chi-squared tests

Below we see type 3 sum of squares tables for R and SAS.

Like before with the linear mixed model results, we are presenting first the results of the unadjusted Cox models which do not account for cage and site. The R results then show the results of the frailty model with a Gaussian distribution of the frailty term. The SAS results show results for both the Gaussian and Gamma frailty term, and as stated above, are generally taken to be more reliable by this authorship team. Further, you’ll note that the SAS frailty model results show two sets of p-values (ProbChiSq) and degrees of freedom. The first set of DF and p-values are calculated not taking the random effect into consideration, while the second set (DF2 and ProbChiSq2) are based on the DF adjustments recommended by (19).

From the SAS tables, we can also check to see if our random effect (here, Cage_site) is significantly explains some of the variation we see in the response - and in this case it does.

R results

To obtain type 3 LR Chi-squared tests in R, we first fit the standard cox model using the coxph() command from the survival library, or the coxme() command from the coxme library for the Cox frailty model. We then use the car package to perform the type 3 test using the Anova() command.

In the R results we see a couple of things. First, that like before with the linear/mixed models, the frailty models show larger p-values. Second, that there again are no significant interactions between treatment and sex, but that we do see significant effects of treatment in the type 3 table for both the standard Cox and Cox frailty models. This means that there is a significant difference in survival based on treatment received, regardless of sex.

library(survival)# load the survival package for fitting the cox model
library(car) # and load the car package for running the anova for the type 3 tests
# fit standard cox model model
cox <- coxph(Surv(Age, Dead) ~ Rx * Sex, data = ITP.data)

# fit the type 3 sum of squares anova for the standard cox model
cox.anova <- Anova(cox, type = 3)
print(cox.anova)

Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
library(coxme) # load the coxme package for the frailty model
# fit the frailty model (Gaussian)
cox.gaus <- coxme(Surv(Age, Dead) ~ Rx*Sex + (1 | Cage_site), data = ITP.data)

# fit the type 3 sum of squares anova for the gaussian frailty model
cox.gaus.anova <- Anova(cox.gaus, type = 3)
print(cox.gaus.anova)

SAS results

In SAS, we can fit standard Cox and Cox frailty models using the PROC PHREG procedure. Like before in the linear/mixed models fit with SAS, a standard Cox model is returned when we omit the random statement. Also like before, we see that the SAS output gives us much more information by default than the R output.

Unlike the R approach, here we see that SAS offers two different distributions for the frailty term - Gamma and log-normal (gaussian). We specify both following the random statement.

Overall, we see that the results from these models are similar to each other and the R results, but not the same. As mentioned previously, it’s our understanding and belief that the SAS Cox frailty models are more robust and reliable than the R results.


/*Below to fit a frailty model on the ITP data, where the model is predicting Age (with 0 as censored animals, and 1 as animals who died) with Rx and Sex, with an interaction between them */

/* as before we are first fitting the cox (and then frailty) models, then extracting the data we want and formating it nicely before printing it in a table */

PROC PHREG data = ITP_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex / param=glm;

   model Age*Dead(0) = Rx|Sex / TYPE3(ALL);

RUN;

PROC PHREG data = ITP_data ;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site Site / param=glm;

   model Age*Dead(0) = Rx|Sex / TYPE3(ALL);

   random Cage_site / dist = GAMMA;

RUN;

/* finally, below to fit the frailty model with a gaussian (lognormal) distribution */

PROC PHREG data = ITP_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site Site / param=glm;

   model Age*Dead(0) = Rx|Sex / TYPE3(ALL);

   random Cage_site / dist = LOGNORMAL;

RUN;

Estimated Marginal Means

Much like before in the linear mixed model results, here we are looking to see if there are any significant survival differences between the treatment groups as compared to the control. Though here because it’s a different model type, we are no longer looking at average survival times and instead are looking at estimated hazard ratios where the hazard is death at any given time, and the ratio is the hazard of death in each treatment group vs. the control. P-values are for the significance of each pairwise treatment comparison vs. the control. Standard errors reported are on the log hazards scale.

R results

As compared to the linear/mixed model estimated marginal means, we see here that the estimates provided (on the “response” scale) are of death hazards as compared to actual numerical days of life. Otherwise, the layout of the R output is largely the same - we see esimates for each treatment within each sex, and pairwise comparsions of each treatment group vs. each other in both male and female animals.

As noted above, we don’t necessarily trust these R results quite as much as the SAS results, but we do see here that male mice treated with Asta, MEC, and MPA have significantly lower hazards of death at any given point in time as compared to the control animals (p = 0.0005, p = 0.007, and p = 0.021) in the standard Cox model. Two of these groups (Asta and MEC) still show significantly lower death hazards in the frailty model (p = 0.001 and p = 0.016) - while the animals treated with MPA no longer show significantly lower death hazards (p = 0.057), indicating again that appropriately accounting for clustering and nesting effects increases p-values.

For the female animals, we see that animals treated with PBA have significantly higher death hazards as compared to control in the Cox model (p = 0.028) but not in the frailty model (p = 0.077) as the p-value increased.

# get the emmeans for the cox model
emm.cox <- emmeans(cox, pairwise ~ Rx | Sex, adjust = "none", type = "response")
print(emm.cox)

SAS results

Like all the SAS output before, we see here that the default SAS code gives us much more information. But, we do see that the overall conclusions of the pairwise comparisons are the same for both the male and female animals. Males treated with Asta, MEC and MPA show significantly reduced death hazards in the standard Cox models, but not the gamma or Gaussian Cox frailty models. Also, females treated with PBA show significantly increased death hazards as compared to control in the Cox model, but not in either Cox frailty model - highlighting again the importance of properly accounting for clustering and nesting effects in your data.


/*Below to fit a frailty model on the ITP data, where the model is predicting Age (with 0 as censored animals, and 1 as animals who died) with Rx and Sex, with an interaction between them */

/* as before we are first fitting the cox (and then frailty) models, then extracting the data we want and formating it nicely before printing it in a table */

PROC PHREG data = ITP_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex / param=glm;

   model Age*Dead(0) = Rx|Sex /;

   lsmeans Rx * Sex / means exp ODDSRATIO diff ;

RUN;

PROC PHREG data = ITP_data;

   class Rx(ref="Cont_19") Sex Cage_site Site / param=glm;

   lsmeans Rx * Sex / means exp ODDSRATIO diff;
